issues.description: The release inventory contains only the datasheet, Stata source and appendix, while the source reads Davila_Guasch_raw.dta, qualtrics_resp.dta and growth_tests_jun21.dta. The main input is described as proprietary with no permission for public sharing; a compatible prepared-table delivery route is unverified. The survey and separate growth-file routes/schema are also unverified. Do not add historical video/handout collection as independent required inputs when the named prepared main table can serve the documented code.

The physical PCA block uses R objects data and data_with_firmid without supplying their construction or exact field/sample mapping, then exports anderson_scoresExpan_all.dta for a Stata firmid merge. The one-speaker rerun and 40–80% pitch score are described/consumed but their full exports and joins are not supplied. The perception PCA has code fragments but no defined survey aggregation, saved score file or Stata handoff; Table 7 reloads Davila_Guasch.dta saved before the physical-score merge and then consumes presence, attract and profession. Table 8 independently loads the growth file with Expan and controls but no merge. Confirm the exact ordered producer-to-consumer contracts without fabricating inputs. The source places the separate OA3 reporting blocks after main Tables 1–10 but signals a Table 7 perception-score prerequisite earlier; the exact manual interleaving and whether later OA3 outputs are reused remain unresolved.

The one-speaker R rerun is said to produce Expan_1speak and Table 3 reports it, but the Stata one-speaker regression panels use Expan; the appendix labels OA4 Panel B as one-speaker expansiveness. Confirm the intended measure/export and branch mapping before changing the scientific specification.

OA4 reads frev_err2, finc_err2 and upmean_ind without producing them in the supplied Stata source. The appendix describes alternative definitions, but repeats the Forecast_Rev_Err2 label in its earnings sentence and does not establish whether the expected columns are already in the unseen prepared table or how they are mapped. Confirm exact source columns and definitions.

Stata 18 and R are available, and eststo/esttab resolve. cluster2 is not found in the active Stata ado path; Petersen's author page links an ado with the same two-cluster option contract, but its file/version was not verified. psych and rio are not found in current R installed-package metadata. Add/configure these required components in a future authorized environment setup. The author does not state required package releases.

The two score merges use a userpath placeholder, while the documented R export writes a named file in the R working directory. Configure Stata and R to share a relative working-copy root and align the named score outputs; this is a supported setup choice, not an unresolved scientific/data blocker.

evidence.description: The survey appendix describes the 1,772 valid unique respondent sample and its response-cleaning conditions.
evidence.quote:
We first asked respondents for their demographic background: age, years of working experience,
education, country of origin and ethnicity. Second, we randomly assigned one video (out of the
154) as a test video, and asked participants to adjust their sound levels. Two questions followed
this test video: a) number of speakers displayed in the clip, and b) a seven-point Likert scale
assessment question on each speaker’s personal characteristic (i.e., dominance, passion,
attractiveness, trustworthiness and competence). This test section ratings were discarded from the
analysis. Next, to reduce concerns related to systematic within-participant response bias, each
respondent only rated three (out of five) randomly assigned personal characteristics, which were
also displayed in random order. Third, the main section of the analysis reproduced the above test
sequence for five randomly assigned videos, making sure no video displayed more than once to
each participant. In addition, no respondent could progress to further sections of the survey until
each video had been completely displayed. Fourth, to validate the quality of the responses, we
introduced two attention check questions by asking respondents to: a) click the “Trustworthy”
option in a question that kept this personal characteristic fixed in the set of responses and, b)
qualitatively explain the task they just performed. As for the latter, we required the presence of
some (root) words that proof diligent participation (e.g., “speak”, “body”, “rate”, “assess”, “trait”,
“present” or “entrepreneur”). We dropped those respondents who failed the above attention check
questions, those who took an excessive time to complete the survey (i.e., more than 15 minutes)
and those who did not finalize the entire video sequence. After the cleaning process, we obtained
1,772 valid unique respondents. The following pages include the survey instrument.

evidence.description: The appendix maps the three PCA components to Presence, Professional and Attractive constructs.
evidence.quote:
The output from the survey generates five significantly correlated behavioral variables. Panel A reports correlations
   for these variables, which are generally above 0.5 (with the exception of attractiveness) and significant at the 1% level.
   We reduce dimensionality using principal component analysis with varimax rotation. 1 While only one component has
   an eigenvalue higher than one, we decided to use three components for the following reasons. Panel B shows that the
   first component captures a high proportion of the original variance (i.e., 66%). Adding a second component increases
   the variance explained to 79% (and to 90% with the inclusion of the third component). Panel C plots the original
   constructs into the first two components space: passionate and dominance load in component 1 (i.e., dots are far from
   the origin in the horizontal axis), attractiveness loads in component 2 (i.e., far from the origin in the vertical axis),
   while trustworthiness and competence bundle together in the middle of the plot. However, three differentiated clusters
   are visually identifiable, which indicates that the use of three components can better reflect the original data. Panel D
   reproduces Panel C analysis in table format using three components. Items that load on the first component are
   dominance and passion, two traits that can make up presence (Cuddy et al. [2013]). We name this factor “Presence.”
   The second component includes trustworthiness and competence, attributes associated with high working standards
   and professionalism (we name this component “Professional”). Finally, attractiveness loads alone in the third
   component (which is consistent with attractiveness being relatively less correlated to the rest of original variables, see
   Panel A), so we name this component “Attractive.”

evidence.description: The appendix describes alternate forecast-error/valuation measures but uses an inconsistent revenue-error label in the earnings sentence.
evidence.quote:
We propose alternative definitions of revenue and earnings forecast errors and high firm
valuations. In particular, we follow Cassar [2010] to define Forecast_Rev_Err2 by comparing
entrepreneurs’ ex ante expectations with actual realizations and scale it by the sum of both:
[(Forecast – Actual) / (Forecast + Actual)]. As for earnings forecast errors, we define
Forecast_Rev_Err2 as the difference between forecasted and actual earnings scaled by size
(number of employees). We convert this variable into €millions for proper coefficient displays in
tables. Finally, for Val_ind2, we reproduce the definition on the paper but compare valuations to
the industry peers mean (instead of financing round). Table OA4.1 provides descriptive statistics
on these alternative measures, and Table OA4.2 reproduces the analysis.

evidence.description: The appendix confirms OA5's outcome, age and VC splits and the survey-derived perception constructs.
evidence.quote:
Table OA5 reports OLS regression coefficients from estimating equation (1) with Forecast_Rev_Err (columns 1, 3,
      5, and 7) and Forecast_Inc_Err (columns 2, 4, 6, and 8) as dependent variables. Columns 1 to 4 split the sample
      according to above/below median firm age (27 months), while columns 5 to 8 do so according to VC presence
      (Yes/No) prior to the investment forum. Columns 1 to 4 include all control variables but Firm age (the splitting
      variable), while columns 5 to 8 omit the VC control variable (the splitting variable). Forecast_Rev_Err is the revenue
      forecast error (classified into quantiles), which compares forecasted to actual revenue numbers and scale it by total
      assets. Forecast_Inc_Err is the income forecast error (classified into quantiles), which compares forecasted to actual
      income numbers and scale it by total assets. Presence, Attractive and Professional have been constructed after a PCA
      on the independent ratings from Turk Prime participants. Presence captures perceptions of dominance and passionate
      characteristics, Attractiveness captures ratings on attractiveness alone, while the Professional component bundles
      perceptions of trustworthiness and competence. Section 3.3 on paper provides further details on the survey and PCA
      variables reduction process. Standard errors are clustered at firm and industry level. *p<0.10, **p<0.05, ***p<0.01
